parts.title: Ordering a birthday cake
parts.context: A woman phones a bakery to order a cake for her mother's birthday party.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a bakery to order a cake. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Good morning, Hilltop Bakery, Sam speaking.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Oh, hello. I'd like to order a cake for my mother's birthday party. She's going to be eighty.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Eighty, how lovely. Let me take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The woman's mother will be eighty, so 'eightieth birthday' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Helen Prentice. That's P-R-E-N-T-I-C-E.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Thank you, Mrs Prentice. Will you collect the cake, or would you like us to deliver it?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Delivery, please. The party's at my house, which is fourteen Orchard Road. Not Orchard Lane, people often mix them up. It's the road just behind the station.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Fourteen Orchard Road. And when is the party?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: It's on Saturday the twelfth of June. Her actual birthday is on the fifth, but my brother can't come until the following weekend.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: And how many people will the cake need to serve?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: We've invited about twenty-five, but my cousins have just told me they're bringing their children, so let's say thirty to be safe.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Thirty. And if we have any questions, what's the best way to contact you? By email?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: I'd rather you sent me a text. I hardly ever check my emails at the weekend.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Now, the cake itself. Most people choose chocolate for a big family party.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: I know, and the children would love that, but it has to be lemon. It's my mother's favourite, and it's her day.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Lemon it is. Are there any allergies we should know about?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Yes, one of my nephews is allergic to nuts, so there mustn't be any nuts at all, not even in the decoration. Eggs and milk are fine.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: No nuts. We can promise that. And how would you like it decorated?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: My mother has grown flowers all her life, especially roses, so I thought some roses made of sugar on the top would be perfect. Pink ones, if possible.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: That will look beautiful. So, the price. A lemon cake for thirty people is seventy pounds, the sugar decoration is another five, and delivery is ten pounds, so that comes to eighty-five pounds altogether.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: That's fine. Do I pay it all now?

script.speaker: sam
script.text: We just ask for a deposit of twenty pounds now, and you pay the rest when the cake is delivered.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Lovely. Can I pay that by card over the phone?

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Of course. I'll take the card details now.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A walking tour of an old harbour town
parts.context: A guide introduces a walking tour of the old town of Wenham.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a tour guide talking to a group of visitors at the start of a walking tour. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Wenham. My name's Clare, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we set off, a few practical things. The leaflet says this walk takes an hour, but with all the stops it's usually closer to two hours, so I hope you're wearing comfortable shoes.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: The streets in the old town are narrow and busy, so it's easy to lose the group. If that happens, please don't try to phone me, because I keep my phone switched off during the tour. And please don't go back to the start. Just make your way to the next stop on your map and wait for us there.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: Now, a little history. Most visitors assume that Wenham grew rich from fishing, as it's on the coast, and there was certainly some fishing here. But the real wealth came from salt, which was produced in shallow pools along the shore and sold all over the country. Wool came later, and it was never as important.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: You'll notice there are very few cars in the old town. Last month the council voted to ban cars from the old town completely, starting next spring. They had considered building a new car park outside the town walls, but in the end it was too expensive.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: Let me tell you about the places we'll visit. Our first stop is the Salt House, where the salt was stored before it was sold. It's now a small museum, but I'm afraid it's shut until the end of the month while the roof is being repaired, so we'll only see it from the outside.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: Next is Saint Peter's Church. A lot of people think the castle ruins are older, but in fact the church tower is the oldest building in the town. It dates from around the year eleven hundred.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: Then we come to the Guildhall, where the merchants used to meet. Some guidebooks say it was designed by a famous London architect, but there's actually no evidence for that. What we do know is that in the eighteenth century the cellars underneath were used to lock up smugglers and thieves, and you can still see the iron rings in the walls.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: After that, we'll climb the hill to the Watch Tower, where guards looked out for ships. There are a hundred and twelve steps, but if you can manage them, you're welcome to climb right to the top. The view is the best in Wenham.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: On the way down, we'll pass the Market Cross. It didn't always stand here. It was originally at the bottom of the hill, and in eighteen ninety it was taken down stone by stone and rebuilt in this square, when the road was widened.

script.speaker: clare
script.text: And our last stop is the Fishermen's Hall, which is now a café. They bake a traditional salt bread there, and you can taste some for free with any drink. It's the perfect place to finish.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A presentation on vertical farming
parts.context: Two agriculture students plan a presentation about a vertical farm they visited.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two agriculture students, Mia and Jack, planning a presentation about a vertical farm they visited. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: So, Mia, the presentation on the vertical farm. What did you think of the visit?

script.speaker: mia
script.text: I loved it. I expected the speed of growth to be the big story, and it was impressive. But what really surprised me was the water. The manager said they use about ninety-five percent less water than a farm in a field.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: Yes, because it's all recycled. OK, how should we start? You suggested a video.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: I did, but after the problems we had with the projector last time, I'd rather not risk it. And we can define vertical farming later.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: Then let's open with a few figures about how much more food the world will need by twenty fifty. That gets people's attention.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: Agreed. Then the disadvantages. The obvious one is that you can't grow everything indoors.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: True, the range of crops is limited, but the real problem is the electricity. The lights are on for sixteen hours a day, and that's where most of their money goes.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: And what about their plans? The manager said they'd tried selling to supermarkets, but the prices were too low.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: Right. So next year they're going to sell straight to restaurants in the city. She said school visits might come later, but not yet.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: Now, how shall we share the work? I could do all the slides, since I enjoy design.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: That's a lot for you. Why don't we each make the slides for the sections we researched, and present those sections ourselves? That seems fairer.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: Fine by me.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: We should also go through the crops they grow. Lettuce first. That's where they started. It was the very first thing they grew, and it's still their biggest crop by weight.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: Then basil. That earns them the most money per kilo, because restaurants pay a lot for fresh herbs.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: And the microgreens, the tiny young plants. They're ready in about ten days, faster than anything else on the farm.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: Tomatoes were the interesting one. There are no bees indoors, so the staff have to pollinate every flower by hand with a little brush.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: And the mushrooms. They don't need any light at all, so they're grown on the bottom shelves, in the dark.

script.speaker: jack
script.text: People used to say customers wouldn't buy vegetables grown indoors, but the manager said that hasn't been a problem with any of them.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: Good point. Let's mention that at the end.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the Inca road network
parts.context: A history lecture about the roads built by the Inca Empire in South America.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the road network of the Inca Empire. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at one of the great engineering achievements of the ancient world, the road network of the Inca Empire, which stretched along the Andes mountains of South America in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The scale is extraordinary. The network covered around thirty thousand kilometres, through deserts, rainforest and some of the highest mountains on Earth. And it was built without the wheel. The Incas knew about circular objects, of course, but wheeled carts would have been useless on such steep ground.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So everything travelled on foot. Goods were carried by people and by llamas, which can carry about thirty kilos each over long distances.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The roads were also the empire's communication system. Messages were carried by teams of runners, who passed them on from one to the next, like a relay race. In this way, news could travel hundreds of kilometres in a single day.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The Incas had no writing as we know it. Instead, information such as population figures and taxes was recorded using knots tied in string, in different colours and positions.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The engineering varied with the landscape. On the steepest mountain slopes, the builders cut steps into the rock, sometimes hundreds of them in a row. Where the roads crossed deep river valleys, they built suspension bridges made of woven grass.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Remarkably, one of these bridges still exists. Every year, local communities gather to weave a new one from fresh grass and take down the old one, a tradition that has continued for over five hundred years.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Along the roads, about every twenty to thirty kilometres, there were way stations. Travellers on official business could rest there, and the stations held stores of food, as well as clothing and weapons for the army.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In twenty fourteen, the road network became a World Heritage Site, shared by six countries. But much of it has been lost. In many places, the old roads now lie under modern highways, which often follow exactly the same routes, because the Inca engineers had already found the best way through the mountains.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
